title: Article Iii Contract Jurisdiction
subject: Constitutional Law
stem: The written installment contract for a small warehouse parcel named Mary as seller and Caleb as buyer. Mary and Caleb are both residents of the same state. After a dispute arose under the contract, Mary filed a $68,400 contract claim against Caleb in a United States district court in that state. Caleb moved to dismiss for lack of jurisdiction. A state statute grants concurrent state and federal jurisdiction over contract disputes, and a federal statute grants jurisdiction to the United States district court to hear this kind of claim.
call: Did the district court have jurisdiction to adjudicate Mary's claim?

choices.A: Yes, because a federal statute grants the United States district court jurisdiction to hear this kind of claim.
choices.B: No, under Article III of the United States Constitution.
choices.C: No, under the Eleventh Amendment to the United States Constitution.
choices.D: Yes, because a state statute grants concurrent state and federal jurisdiction over contract disputes.

rightExplanation: The district court lacked jurisdiction. Article III defines the outer limits of federal judicial power. It permits federal jurisdiction only for enumerated categories, such as federal-question cases, diversity controversies, and certain other listed disputes. Mary's claim is an ordinary contract dispute between residents of the same state. No fact places it within an Article III category. A state statute cannot give a federal court constitutional judicial power. A federal statute also cannot authorize jurisdiction beyond Article III. Because Article III does not permit this case, dismissal is proper.

wrongExplanations.A: The federal statute is the strongest lure because Congress ordinarily defines lower federal court jurisdiction. The breaker is that Congress may grant only jurisdiction Article III permits.
wrongExplanations.C: The Eleventh Amendment sounds constitutional and jurisdictional. The breaker is that Mary sued Caleb, not a state, so sovereign immunity is not the problem.
wrongExplanations.D: Concurrent state and federal jurisdiction language makes the state statute seem enabling. The breaker is that state law cannot expand the constitutional judicial power of federal courts.
